posts.text:
The US deficit isn’t a revenue problem—it’s a spending problem. Taxes on the wealthy or new levies won’t fix deficits: high taxes shrink the base, and 98% of revenue shortfalls come from unchecked government spending, says Cato’s @veroderugy.
ow.ly/GNjU50YC3MG

The government has illegally collected more than $160 billion in IEEPA tariffs. Now, US taxpayers are on the hook for about $700 million in additional interest payments for every month that refunds are delayed, according to Cato Institute scholars. 

ow.ly/fu5050YCwb8

Cato’s @foxmike90 warns of a growing “remedy-free zone,” where legal doctrines shield federal agents from accountability. State statutory remedies are a way to push back, but Fox warns that a guaranteed and consistent accountability mechanism ultimately requires congressional action.
ow.ly/molf50YClzY

Can the government permanently strip someone of their Second Amendment rights for a past felony? 

Cato joined an amicus brief with the ACLU of North Carolina Legal Foundation, arguing that North Carolina’s blanket firearm ban for all felons—regardless of violence, history, or time since conviction—is unconstitutional. 
ow.ly/zUEM50YBSlW

The data confirm that—contrary to White House promises—there was no tariff-related hiring boom in 2025, Cato scholars report. 

ow.ly/yIb350YCvHK

TSA agents staying home, hours-long airport lines, and Congress still cannot agree on a DHS funding bill. Cato’s Pat Eddington and @CatoEdwards say this is a consequence of tying aviation security to the federal budget, a mistake other high-income countries do not make.
 
Listen to the new Cato Podcast episode!
 
Apple: ow.ly/txu850YCoAA
Spotify: ow.ly/74RA50YCoAB
Our website: ow.ly/BbYA50YCoAz

Despite the president’s “Liberation Day” prediction of a boom in foreign direct investment, quarterly FDI has fallen since April 2025, Cato scholars report. 

Total FDI in 2025 was $288.4B, lower than the annual totals from 2021 through 2024, and far short of the rate needed to reach the president’s goal of $18T in investment.  

ow.ly/SF5C50YCw2z

One year ago today, President Trump celebrated “Liberation Day,” unveiling his global “reciprocal” tariffs. 
  
Safe to say, things didn’t work out as promised, Cato scholars write. 
  
Check out the detailed overview based on 12 months of data from Cato’s @scottlincicome, @AlfredCObregon, and Chad Smitson: 
ow.ly/2TfX50YCv7n

President Trump’s decision to pay TSA workers, despite a funding lapse, offers short‑term relief but long‑term risk. If the executive branch is now allowed to spend without congressional appropriation, then Congress’s exclusive power of the purse becomes meaningless, says Cato’s Molly Nixon. 

ow.ly/53Mk50YBZxl

Some have urged Britain and France to extend their nuclear umbrellas, but that path risks instability. Europe’s safer course is to build strong conventional defenses, not rely on fragile nuclear guarantees, argues @GiltnerBen.
 
ow.ly/t1yo50YBZ3H

If Congress is serious about lowering housing costs, it should fix the tax code—not layer on more subsidies. Current depreciation rules discourage building. Full expensing or better cost recovery would boost supply. No supply, no affordability, explains Cato’s @adamnmichel.  
ow.ly/c9y050YC34M

When the government takes ownership stakes in private companies, it distorts free markets and weakens economic freedom. With the state acting like an investor, market discipline erodes, and political favoritism takes its place, says Cato’s @DeHavenTad.

ow.ly/tERt50YBUOE

If the Fed controls interest rates, why do rates change when the Fed does nothing? 

That’s because markets—not the Fed—ultimately determine interest rates, Cato’s @norbertjmichel and @JaiKedia explain. 
ow.ly/a0m550YC3q6

HB 649 passed the MD House 100–35. It would let the State Commission on Civil Rights enforce nondiscrimination rules on private schools—even if those rules run counter to a school’s religious teachings. Cato's @ColleenHroncich says supporters of educational freedom must stay vigilant.
ow.ly/IL8U50YC3PY

"Chief Justice Roberts had the line of the morning when he said, ‘It's a new world, but it's the same Constitution.' That really does sum up why the government's policy-based arguments had no bearing on the constitutional question,” says Cato’s @Thomas_A_Berry, commenting on the birthright citizenship SCOTUS case.
Ending or curtailing birthright citizenship would imperil the rights of every natural-born American citizen, regardless of ancestry, says the Cato Institute’s @David_J_Bier.

Justice Barrett highlighted that the Trump administration's rationales for denying birthright citizenship would have also denied it to numerous freed slaves and their children—contradicting the original purpose of the Citizenship Clause. This alone is enough to reject the administration’s claim, says @IlyaSomin. 

Learn more: ow.ly/GePr50YC2Jz
